newsitem.title: FRANCE: MEPs say Council wrecked health monitoring scheme.
newsitem.headline: MEPs say Council wrecked health monitoring scheme.

text.p: The European Parliament attacked EU health ministers on Wednesday, saying they had practically sabotaged plans for an EU system to monitor the spread of cancer, AIDS and other major illnesses.

Giving the plans a second reading, MEPs accused the member states of reneging on their EU treaty commitment to ensure "a high level of human health protection" by coordinating their efforts to prevent disease and improve health information.

The European Commission has proposed a five-year EU action programme for monitoring health indicators -- COM(96)222 -- but the Council's common position on the text emptied it of substance, Parliament complained in a report by Italian Christian Democrat Danilo Poggiolini.

MEPs were furious that ministers had axed the programme's budget, refused to harmonise national health indicators or set up a permanent, central health monitoring structure and had imposed a costly and bureaucratic administrative structure on the programme.
"The governments of the member states are guilty of alarming shortsightedness," and are preventing the development of an EU policy on public health, the Parliament's report said.
MEPs reinstated amendments to the draft decision which they made at first reading on April 17 but which health ministers threw out when they adopted their common position on May 14.

At first reading, parliament reduced its original demand for a budget of 35 million Ecus for the programme to 20 million Ecus. MEPs refused on Wednesday to compromise further and insisted the 20 million figure should be retained.

The Council's decision to give the programme 13 million Ecus amounted to "insulting" penny-pinching and made little sense since an efficient and cost-effective EU disease prevention mechanism would help governments reduce their astronomical health budgets, the report argued.
Parliament also insisted on the need for the member states to use the same technical language.
In a situation in which even the definition "hospital bed" meant different things in different countries, it was impossible to compare national health indicators, the report said.

The Council had rejected this idea on the grounds that the EU treaty chapter on public health policy (Title X) explicitly excluded "any harmonisation of the laws and regulations of the member states".
But Parliament's report pointed out MEPs were only suggesting a harmonisation of technical, medical and sanitary definitions.

Parliament also reintroduced a demand, refused by Council, for a study to examine the feasibility of setting up a permanent European health observatory which would collect and analyse national health indicators.

EU action on health could be made even more efficient, Parliament said, if the committee set up to help the Commission run the monitoring programme were made up of one expert from each of the 15 member states.
Ministers said there should be two representatives per country.
